newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pivotal role may not give French Communists power.
newsitem.headline: Pivotal role may not give French Communists power.

text.p: France's Communist party will hold the balance of power in theory in the new parliament, but if history is any guide, that may not give them much leverage over the policies of a Socialist-led government.

With all but 10 constituencies declared, the non-communist left was certain to fall short of an absolute majority in the 577-seat National Assembly, although it will have significantly more seats than the combined centre-right.
The 38 Communist deputies potentially hold a pivotal role.
But the Fifth Republic constitution gives the government broad powers to legislate by decree or use confidence motions to ram legislation through a recalcitrant parliament.

The Socialists ran minority governments from 1988 to 1993 without Communist participation, relying on the Communists to either support some bills, abstain on others or refuse to back right-wing no-confidence motions when things came to a head.

Then-prime minister Michel Rocard lost one or two minor votes in the National Assembly but was able to use Article 49-3 of the constitution to force budgets through the lower house by turning them into confidence votes.
However, the Socialists may have more difficulty using this device, sometimes called the government's nuclear deterrent, in a period of powersharing with Gaullist President Jacques Chirac.

The constitution requires the president to authorise the prime minister to "engage the government's responsibility" in parliament, the equivalent of challenging the opposition to bring the cabinet down.
The opposition then has 48 hours to table a censure motion. If it does not do so, or if the motion fails to win an absolute majority of 289 votes, the bill is deemed to have passed.

Chirac was exposed to some of the president's blocking powers and delaying tactics when he was prime minister under Socialist Francois Mitterrand during the first period of left-right "cohabitation" from 1986 to 1988, and he can be expected to use them to his advantage.
In 1986, Mitterrand refused to sign decrees speeding up privatisation and abolishing a requirement on private companies to seek government permission to make redundancies.
That forced Chirac to take the slower route of putting the measures through parliament as bills. Since he had a majority, their passage was assured.

The new left-wing government may also face delays in legislation because the centre-right continues to control the Senate, the upper house of parliament, which can obstruct and slow but ultimately not block bills.
The National Assembly has the final say on a second reading.
